```{r prep, echo = TRUE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
library(tidyverse)
library(magrittr)
library(gtrendsR)
library(ggplot2)
library(sf)
library(gtrendsR)
library(tigris)
library(tidymodels)
library(igraph)
theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 13))
```

```{r google trends, echo = TRUE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
# This section uses Google Trends as a digital trace of cultural attention.
# The values are relative, with 100 representing peak search interest in the selected time period.

reggaeton_trends <- gtrends(c("reggaeton"),
                            geo = "US",
                            time = "all")
reggaeton_time <- reggaeton_trends$interest_over_time
reggaeton_time %<>%
  mutate(hits = ifelse(hits == "<1", "0", hits),
         hits = as.numeric(hits))
ggplot(reggaeton_time, aes(x = date, y = hits)) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.7) +
  # The LOESS creates a smooth curve to follow to see google search trends easier
  geom_smooth(se = FALSE, method = "loess") +
  labs(title = "Reggaeton Search Interest Rose Unevenly Over Time",
       subtitle = "Google Trends data, United States, 2004-present",
       x = "Year",
       y = "Relative Search Interest",
       caption = "Note: Google Trends values are relative, where 100 represents peak interest in the selected period.") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)
```





```{r search-interest-events, echo = TRUE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
# Reggaeton search interest with major cultural moments
# This adds important cultural moments to the time-series graph.
# These events of different top song release dates help connect changes in the data to real-world music history.
events <- data.frame(
  event_date = as.Date(c("2004-07-13", "2017-01-12", "2020-02-29",
                         "2022-05-06", "2023-02-24")),
  event = c("Gasolina", "Despacito", "YHLQMDLG",
            "Un Verano Sin Ti", "Mañana Será Bonito")
)
ggplot(reggaeton_time, aes(x = date, y = hits)) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.8) +
  geom_vline(data = events,
             aes(xintercept = event_date),
             linetype = "dashed",
             alpha = 0.6) +
  # I worked to specifify the look of this graph to be easiest readible to viewers
  geom_text(data = events,
            aes(x = event_date, y = 95, label = event),
            angle = 90,
            vjust = 1.2,
            hjust = 1,
            size = 3) +
  labs(title = "Major Cultural Moments Created Visibility Shocks",
       subtitle = "Key songs and albums are marked on the Google Trends timeline",
       x = "Year",
       y = "Relative Search Interest") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)
```


```{r by-state-search, echo = TRUE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
# Google Trends data by state
# This section uses Google Trends geography data.
# I use the past 5 years because Google Trends geographic data is more stable and easier to interpret over a recent time period.

reggaeton_geo <- gtrends(c("reggaeton"),
                         geo = "US",
                         time = "today+5-y")

geo_state <- reggaeton_geo$interest_by_region

geo_state %<>%
  rename(NAME = location) %>%
  mutate(hits = ifelse(hits == "<1", "0", hits),
         hits = as.numeric(hits))

head(geo_state)
```


```{r map, echo = TRUE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
# Map og reggaeton search interest by state
# This follows the spatial analysis skills I learned from class using tigris and ggplot.
# The map shows where reggaeton search interest is highest across the U.S.

states_data <- states(cb = TRUE)

#remove these states to solely include mainland states
states_data %<>%
  filter(!STUSPS %in% c("AK", "HI", "PR"))

states_reggaeton <- left_join(states_data, geo_state, by = "NAME")

ggplot(states_reggaeton) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = hits), color = "white", linewidth = 0.1) +
  coord_sf(xlim = c(-125, -66),
           ylim = c(24, 50),
           expand = FALSE) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "magma", na.value = "gray90") +
  labs(title = "Reggaeton Search Interest by State",
       subtitle = "Google Trends data, past 5 years",
       fill = "Search\nInterest",
       caption = "Alaska, Hawaii, and Puerto Rico removed for visual clarity.") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(axis.text = element_blank(),
        axis.title = element_blank(),
        axis.ticks = element_blank(),
        panel.grid = element_blank(),
        plot.caption = element_text(hjust = 0))
```




```{r net, echo = TRUE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
## Artist collaboration network
# This section is my a small hand-coded collaboration dataset.
# It follows the same igraph approach from the class network problem set.
# The point is to show social/network connections between artists.

collabs <- data.frame(
  artist_1 = c("Bad Bunny", "Bad Bunny", "Bad Bunny", "J Balvin",
               "Karol G", "Daddy Yankee", "Daddy Yankee",
               "J Balvin", "Nicky Jam", "Ozuna"),
  artist_2 = c("J Balvin", "Daddy Yankee", "Karol G", "Daddy Yankee",
               "Nicki Minaj", "Nicky Jam", "Ozuna",
               "Willy William", "Daddy Yankee", "Bad Bunny")
)

reggaeton_net <- graph_from_data_frame(collabs, directed = FALSE)

V(reggaeton_net)$degree <- degree(reggaeton_net)

plot(reggaeton_net,
     vertex.size = V(reggaeton_net)$degree * 8 + 10,
     vertex.color = "lavender",
     vertex.frame.color = NA,
     vertex.label.cex = .8,
     edge.curved = .05,
     edge.width = 1,
     edge.color = "gray50",
     main = "Reggaeton Collaboration Network")

degree(reggaeton_net)
```


```{r artist-case-data, echo = TRUE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
# This section creates the artist-level case dataset used for the positive/negative case comparison.
# The variables compare Billboard visibility, collaboration activity, and peak Google Trends attention.

artist_data <- tibble(
  artist = c("Bad Bunny", "Karol G", "J Balvin", "Daddy Yankee",
             "Ozuna", "Nicky Jam", "Arcangel", "De La Ghetto",
             "Ñengo Flow", "Jowell y Randy"),
```

```{r load-billboard, echo=TRUE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
# This public GitHub dataset archives Billboard Hot 100 chart data.
# I use it as a second data source because Google Trends measures search attention,
# while Billboard measures mainstream chart visibility.

billboard_url <- "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/utdata/rwd-billboard-data/main/data-out/hot-100-current.csv"

billboard <- read_csv(billboard_url)

head(billboard)
names(billboard)

```
```{r billboard-clean, echo = TRUE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
# Clean Billboard data for the selected reggaeton and Latin urbano artist cases.
# The Billboard file has one row per song per chart week, so I collapse it to artist-level visibility measures.

reggaeton_artists <- c("Bad Bunny", "Karol G", "Daddy Yankee", "J Balvin",
                       "Nicky Jam", "Ozuna", "Ñengo Flow", "De La Ghetto",
                       "Jowell y Randy", "Arcangel")

billboard_reggaeton <- billboard %>%
  filter(str_detect(performer, str_c(reggaeton_artists, collapse = "|"))) %>%
  mutate(year = as.numeric(format(as.Date(chart_week), "%Y")))

billboard_reggaeton %>%
  select(chart_week, year, title, performer, current_week, peak_pos, wks_on_chart) %>%
  head()

billboard_artist_summary <- data.frame()

for (artist in reggaeton_artists) {
  
  artist_rows <- billboard %>%
    filter(str_detect(performer, artist))
  
  artist_summary <- data.frame(
    artist = artist,
    billboard_entries = nrow(artist_rows),
    unique_songs = n_distinct(artist_rows$title),
    best_peak_position = min(artist_rows$peak_pos, na.rm = TRUE),
    total_weeks_on_chart = sum(artist_rows$wks_on_chart, na.rm = TRUE)
  )
  
  billboard_artist_summary <- bind_rows(billboard_artist_summary,
                                        artist_summary)
}

billboard_artist_summary %<>%
  mutate(best_peak_position = ifelse(is.infinite(best_peak_position),
                                     NA,
                                     best_peak_position),
         mainstream = ifelse(artist %in% c("Bad Bunny", "Karol G",
                                           "Daddy Yankee", "J Balvin",
                                           "Nicky Jam", "Ozuna"),
                             "yes", "no"))

billboard_artist_summary

```

```{r billboard-over-time, echo=TRUE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}

# This uses Reggaeton Music in Billboard Hot 100 to show growth of the genre overtime 
billboard_yearly <- billboard_reggaeton %>%
  group_by(year) %>%
  summarize(entries = n(),
            unique_songs = n_distinct(title))

ggplot(billboard_yearly, aes(x = year, y = unique_songs)) +
  geom_line(size = 1) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(title = "Reggaeton-Related Billboard Hot 100 Visibility Over Time",
       subtitle = "Number of unique songs by selected reggaeton artists appearing each year",
       x = "Year",
       y = "Unique Hot 100 Songs") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)
```




```{r billboard-artist-visibility, echo=TRUE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}


# The first graph, “Billboard Hot 100 Visibility by Artist,” compares reggaeton and Latin urban artists based on how many distinct songs they have had appear on the 
# Billboard Hot 100. Since the artists are ranked by their number of unique Hot 100 songs, the graph makes it easy to see which artists have had the most mainstream chart
# visibility. I chose for  fill color separates artists classified as mainstream from those classified as less mainstream, showing not only which artists appear most often on the
# chart, but also how Billboard visibility is distributed across different levels of mainstream recognition. Overall, this graph highlights that Hot 100 visibility is not
# evenly spread across all artists, but is concentrated among a smaller group of highly visible performers.
billboard_yearly <- billboard_reggaeton %>%
  group_by(year) %>%
  summarize(entries = n(),
            unique_songs = n_distinct(title))


ggplot(billboard_artist_summary,
       aes(x = reorder(artist, unique_songs),
           y = unique_songs,
           fill = mainstream)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity") +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(title = "Billboard Hot 100 Visibility by Artist",
       subtitle = "Distinct songs appearing on the Billboard Hot 100",
       x = "Artist",
       y = "Unique Hot 100 Songs",
       fill = "Mainstream") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)

# The second graph, “Billboard Visibility Is Concentrated Among a Few
# Artists,” shows the cumulative share of Billboard Hot 100 visibility by artist rank. Artists are ordered from highest to lowest visibility, and the curve shows how quickly
# the total share of unique Hot 100 songs accumulates as more artists are added. A steep rise at the beginning of the curve would mean that the top-ranked artists account for
# a large portion of all Billboard visibility, while a flatter curve would suggest a more even distribution. In this case, the graph is meant to demonstrate that Billboard
# success in reggaeton is highly concentrated, with a relatively small number of artists making up a large share of the genre’s mainstream Hot 100 presence.


billboard_visibility_curve <- billboard_artist_summary %>%
  arrange(desc(unique_songs)) %>%
  mutate(rank = row_number(),
         total_visibility = sum(unique_songs),
         cumulative_visibility = cumsum(unique_songs),
         cumulative_share = cumulative_visibility / total_visibility)

ggplot(billboard_visibility_curve, aes(x = rank, y = cumulative_share)) +
  geom_line(size = 1) +
  geom_point() +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(title = "Billboard Visibility Is Concentrated Among a Few Artists",
       subtitle = "Cumulative share of unique Hot 100 songs by artist rank",
       x = "Artist Rank by Billboard Visibility",
       y = "Cumulative Share of Billboard Visibility") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)

```


```{r billboard-rf-importance, echo = TRUE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
#This code builds a random forest model to predict whether selected reggaeton and Latin urban songs reached the Billboard Hot 100 Top 10. 
#It starts by loading Billboard chart data, filtering for a set of Latin artists, and summarizing the weekly chart records into one row per artist-song case. 
#The code then creates a Top 10 outcome variable and several predictors, including first charting year, weeks on chart, number of chart entries, collaboration status, and 
# mainstream artist status. Finally, it fits a random forest model and plots variable importance to show which predictors mattered most for classifying Top 10 success.

billboard_url <- "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/utdata/rwd-billboard-data/main/data-out/hot-100-current.csv"

billboard <- read_csv(billboard_url)

latin_artists <- c("Bad Bunny", "Karol G", "Daddy Yankee", "J Balvin",
                   "Nicky Jam", "Ozuna", "Arcangel", "Anuel AA",
                   "Rauw Alejandro", "Farruko", "Feid", "Myke Towers",
                   "Wisin", "Yandel", "Don Omar", "Tego Calderon",
                   "Chencho Corleone", "Plan B", "Sech",
                   "Natti Natasha", "Eladio Carrion", "Mora")

billboard_latin <- data.frame()

for (artist in latin_artists) {
  
  artist_rows <- billboard %>%
    filter(str_detect(performer, regex(artist, ignore_case = TRUE))) %>%
    mutate(artist = artist)
  
  billboard_latin <- bind_rows(billboard_latin, artist_rows)
}

billboard_latin %<>%
  mutate(chart_week = as.Date(chart_week),
         year = as.numeric(format(chart_week, "%Y")))

song_level <- billboard_latin %>%
  group_by(artist, title, performer) %>%
  summarize(first_year = min(year, na.rm = TRUE),
            best_peak_position = min(peak_pos, na.rm = TRUE),
            max_weeks_on_chart = max(wks_on_chart, na.rm = TRUE),
            chart_entries = n(),
            .groups = "drop") %>%
  mutate(top_10 = ifelse(best_peak_position <= 10, "yes", "no"),
         top_10 = factor(top_10, levels = c("no", "yes")),
         collaboration = ifelse(str_detect(performer, "Featuring|Feat\\.|feat\\.|,|&| x | X "),
                                "yes", "no"),
         collaboration = as.factor(collaboration),
         mainstream_artist = ifelse(artist %in% c("Bad Bunny", "Karol G",
                                                  "Daddy Yankee", "J Balvin",
                                                  "Nicky Jam", "Ozuna",
                                                  "Rauw Alejandro"),
                                    "yes", "no"),
         mainstream_artist = as.factor(mainstream_artist))

song_model_data <- song_level %>%
  select(top_10,
         first_year,
         max_weeks_on_chart,
         chart_entries,
         collaboration,
         mainstream_artist) %>%
  drop_na()

song_recipe <- recipe(top_10 ~ ., data = song_model_data) %>%
  step_dummy(all_nominal_predictors())

rf_model_importance <-
  rand_forest(trees = 500) %>%
  set_engine("ranger", importance = "impurity") %>%
  set_mode("classification")

rf_wflow_importance <-
  workflow() %>%
  add_recipe(song_recipe) %>%
  add_model(rf_model_importance)

rf_fit_importance <- fit(rf_wflow_importance,
                         data = song_model_data)

rf_importance <- rf_fit_importance %>%
  extract_fit_parsnip() %>%
  pluck("fit", "variable.importance") %>%
  as.data.frame()

rf_importance$variable <- rownames(rf_importance)

names(rf_importance)[1] <- "importance"

ggplot(rf_importance, aes(x = reorder(variable, importance),
                          y = importance)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity") +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(title = "Random Forest Variable Importance",
       subtitle = "Which features mattered most for classifying Top 10 success?",
       x = "Predictor",
       y = "Importance") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)
```
